units.title: Real-Time Fundamentals
units.tip: A real-time system is one where correctness depends on both the result and the time it is produced. Timing deadlines are not optional; they are part of the specification.

exercises.question: What defines a real-time system?
exercises.answer: Correctness depends on the result and the time it is delivered
exercises.explain: A real-time system must not only produce the right answer but deliver it by a deadline. Lateness is failure, even if the answer is correct.
choices: It runs at the fastest speed possible
Correctness depends on the result and the time it is delivered
It processes data in real time on live input
It requires 100% uptime with no errors

exercises.question: What is the primary challenge in real-time computing?
exercises.answer: Meeting strict timing constraints predictably
exercises.explain: Real-time systems must guarantee that tasks complete within their deadlines. The challenge is making this guarantee even under worst-case conditions.
choices: Maximizing the total throughput of the system
Reducing memory usage
Processing data faster than other systems
Meeting strict timing constraints predictably

exercises.question: Why is predictability more important than speed in real-time systems?
exercises.answer: A slow but predictable system can meet deadlines; a fast but unpredictable one cannot
exercises.explain: In real-time computing, knowing that a task will finish in 50ms is more valuable than knowing it sometimes finishes in 10ms and sometimes in 100ms.
choices: Slow systems are always more reliable
Speed is never important
A slow but predictable system can meet deadlines; a fast but unpredictable one cannot
Real-time systems do not care about performance

exercises.question: In a hard real-time system, what happens if a task misses its deadline?
exercises.answer: The system has failed, even if the result was eventually correct
exercises.explain: Missing a deadline is a failure of the real-time system, regardless of whether the computation was correct. The late result is useless.
choices: The system has failed, even if the result was eventually correct
The result is discarded
Nothing happens; the system retries the task
The system attempts to recover the lost time

exercises.question: What is a 'timing constraint' in real-time systems?
exercises.answer: A specification of when a task or event must be completed
exercises.explain: Timing constraints are deadlines, period requirements, and latency bounds written into the system specification. They are requirements, not suggestions.
choices: A hardware limitation of the CPU
The time it takes to reboot the system
A specification of when a task or event must be completed
The maximum amount of data a task can process

exercises.question: What is a hard real-time deadline?
exercises.answer: A deadline that must be met; missing it causes complete system failure
exercises.explain: Hard deadlines are unforgiving. A missile guidance system, pacemaker, or aircraft autopilot cannot tolerate a missed deadline.
choices: A deadline that the system tries to meet
A deadline that can be missed occasionally
A deadline that is less strict than average
A deadline that must be met; missing it causes complete system failure

exercises.question: What is a soft real-time deadline?
exercises.answer: A deadline that is desirable but missing it degrades service, not fails the system
exercises.explain: Soft deadlines are common in multimedia and interactive systems. Streaming video can drop frames; audio can skip. The system keeps running.
choices: A deadline that is desirable but missing it degrades service, not fails the system
A deadline that is never important
A deadline that is twice as long as a hard deadline
A deadline that must be met

exercises.question: Which example is a hard real-time system?
exercises.answer: An aircraft's autopilot control system
exercises.explain: Aircraft control must respond to sensor input within strict deadlines. A late response can cause a crash. Streaming video or web page loading can tolerate delays.
choices: A web page that takes 5 seconds to load
An aircraft's autopilot control system
A background file sync process
A video streaming service buffering a frame

exercises.question: Which example is a soft real-time system?
exercises.answer: A video game rendering frames at 60fps
exercises.explain: Video games aim for smooth frame rates but can drop a frame or two without crashing. Users perceive degradation, but the system continues.
choices: A brake-by-wire system in a car
A surgical robot controlling a scalpel
A nuclear plant emergency shutdown
A video game rendering frames at 60fps

exercises.question: Why must hard real-time systems be designed differently from soft real-time systems?
exercises.answer: Hard systems must guarantee deadlines in the worst case; soft systems only aim for average performance
exercises.explain: Hard real-time systems use worst-case timing analysis, dedicated hardware, and predictable scheduling. Soft systems can use best-effort scheduling.
choices: Hard systems are always more expensive
Soft systems are easier to implement
There is no difference in design approach
Hard systems must guarantee deadlines in the worst case; soft systems only aim for average performance

units.title: Tasks, Priorities, and Scheduling
units.tip: A real-time system executes multiple tasks with different priorities and deadlines. The scheduler decides which task runs at each moment. Good scheduling ensures all tasks meet their deadlines.

exercises.question: What is a 'task' in real-time systems?
exercises.answer: A unit of work with a specific deadline and priority
exercises.explain: A task is a schedulable unit in a real-time system. Each task has timing requirements (deadline, period) and a priority level.
choices: Any process running on the computer
A thread that never blocks
A unit of work with a specific deadline and priority
A piece of hardware

exercises.question: What is a 'periodic task'?
exercises.answer: A task that executes repeatedly at fixed time intervals
exercises.explain: A periodic task has a period. It might execute every 10ms, every 100ms, or every second. Real-time control loops are periodic.
choices: A task that completes in periodic timing
A task that has a deadline
A task that executes repeatedly at fixed time intervals
A task that uses periodic memory

exercises.question: What is an 'aperiodic task'?
exercises.answer: A task that is triggered irregularly, not at fixed intervals
exercises.explain: Aperiodic tasks respond to events. An interrupt handler processing a button press is aperiodic; it activates only when the button is pressed.
choices: A task that is triggered irregularly, not at fixed intervals
A task that is never periodic
A task that has no deadline
A task with very low priority

exercises.question: What does 'task priority' mean in a real-time scheduler?
exercises.answer: A ranking that determines which task runs when multiple tasks are ready
exercises.explain: Higher priority tasks run first. If a high-priority task becomes ready while a low-priority one is running, the scheduler preempts the low-priority task.
choices: How important the task is to the user
Which task started first
A ranking that determines which task runs when multiple tasks are ready
How long the task will take

exercises.question: In a priority-driven scheduler, what happens when a higher-priority task becomes ready?
exercises.answer: The lower-priority task is preempted and the higher-priority task runs
exercises.explain: Preemption allows the scheduler to interrupt a running task and switch to a higher-priority one. This ensures urgent work is not delayed.
choices: Nothing; the lower-priority task continues
The lower-priority task waits until the next time slice
Both tasks run together
The lower-priority task is preempted and the higher-priority task runs

exercises.question: What is 'Rate Monotonic' scheduling?
exercises.answer: Assign higher priority to tasks with shorter periods
exercises.explain: In Rate Monotonic, a task with a 10ms period gets higher priority than a task with a 100ms period. This simple rule provably meets all deadlines under certain conditions.
choices: Assign priority by task size
Assign higher priority to tasks with shorter periods
Assign priority randomly
Assign priority by task creation time

exercises.question: What is 'Earliest Deadline First' (EDF) scheduling?
exercises.answer: At any moment, run the task with the soonest deadline
exercises.explain: EDF is dynamic: deadlines change as time passes. The task closest to missing its deadline gets the CPU. EDF is optimal for uniprocessor scheduling.
choices: Run the shortest task first
Run tasks in the order they arrive
Run all deadlines at the same time
At any moment, run the task with the soonest deadline

exercises.question: What is an advantage of Rate Monotonic over other schemes?
exercises.answer: It is simple, static, and easy to verify offline
exercises.explain: Rate Monotonic requires no dynamic decisions at runtime. You assign priorities once, and analysis can prove all deadlines are met before deployment.
choices: It uses less memory
It always runs faster than other algorithms
It handles aperiodic tasks better
It is simple, static, and easy to verify offline

exercises.question: What is an advantage of Earliest Deadline First over Rate Monotonic?
exercises.answer: EDF can schedule tasks that Rate Monotonic cannot, achieving higher CPU utilization
exercises.explain: EDF is optimal: if any scheduling algorithm can meet all deadlines, EDF will. Rate Monotonic is less flexible but simpler to analyze.
choices: EDF can schedule tasks that Rate Monotonic cannot, achieving higher CPU utilization
EDF uses less memory
EDF does not require priorities
EDF is always faster

exercises.question: In EDF, if two tasks have the same deadline, what happens?
exercises.answer: The scheduler chooses between them arbitrarily; the system design should avoid ties
exercises.explain: EDF does not define behavior for tied deadlines. Real systems break ties by secondary priority, FIFO, or other rules. Designers should avoid exact deadline ties.
choices: Both run at the same time
The system crashes
The task with higher priority runs
The scheduler chooses between them arbitrarily; the system design should avoid ties

units.title: Priority Inversion and Synchronization
units.tip: When a low-priority task locks a resource that a high-priority task needs, the high-priority task is blocked. This priority inversion can cause deadline misses. Solutions include priority inheritance and priority ceiling protocols.

exercises.question: What is 'priority inversion'?
exercises.answer: A low-priority task blocks a high-priority task, inverting the effective priorities
exercises.explain: Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority task waits for a resource held by a low-priority task. The high-priority task is effectively delayed as if it had low priority.
choices: A hardware failure in the scheduler
A low-priority task blocks a high-priority task, inverting the effective priorities
When task priorities are assigned randomly
When the high-priority task finishes first

exercises.question: Why is priority inversion dangerous in real-time systems?
exercises.answer: The high-priority task may miss its deadline while waiting for the low-priority task
exercises.explain: If a critical, high-priority task is blocked by a less critical task, it may miss its deadline. In hard real-time, this is a system failure.
choices: It increases memory usage
It causes data corruption
It makes the system slower
The high-priority task may miss its deadline while waiting for the low-priority task

exercises.question: In a priority inversion scenario, what blocks the high-priority task?
exercises.answer: The low-priority task holding a mutex or semaphore it needs
exercises.explain: The high-priority task tries to acquire a lock (mutex, semaphore) that the low-priority task already holds. Synchronization primitives, meant to protect data, cause the inversion.
choices: The scheduler bug
Another high-priority task
A hardware interrupt
The low-priority task holding a mutex or semaphore it needs

exercises.question: What is the 'unbounded priority inversion' problem?
exercises.answer: The duration of blocking is unpredictable because intermediate tasks can extend the delay
exercises.explain: If a third task runs between the blocking and the resource holder, it adds more delay. Without limits, the high-priority task's latency becomes unbounded.
choices: The inversion lasts forever
The duration of blocking is unpredictable because intermediate tasks can extend the delay
The priority levels are infinite
Multiple priority inversions happen at once

exercises.question: What famous incident highlighted the dangers of priority inversion?
exercises.answer: The Mars Pathfinder rover experiencing spontaneous resets due to priority inversion
exercises.explain: In 1997, Mars Pathfinder kept resetting itself. A low-priority task held a shared mutex needed by a high-priority bus task, and medium-priority tasks kept preempting the holder. The watchdog saw the stall and reset the system.
choices: A smartphone crashing during a call
A website going offline
The Mars Pathfinder rover experiencing spontaneous resets due to priority inversion
An ATM running out of money

exercises.question: What is 'priority inheritance'?
exercises.answer: When a lower-priority task holds a lock, it temporarily inherits the priority of the highest-priority task waiting for that lock
exercises.explain: Priority inheritance ensures that the low-priority task holding a resource runs at high enough priority to release it quickly, reducing blocking time.
choices: Giving all tasks the same priority
When a lower-priority task holds a lock, it temporarily inherits the priority of the highest-priority task waiting for that lock
Copying one task's priority to another
A hardware mechanism in the CPU

exercises.question: How does priority inheritance reduce priority inversion?
exercises.answer: The low-priority task runs at high priority while holding the lock, executing and releasing it quickly
exercises.explain: By elevating the low-priority task's priority, it is not preempted by other medium-priority tasks. It runs to completion and releases the lock sooner.
choices: It removes the high-priority task
It pauses all other tasks
The low-priority task runs at high priority while holding the lock, executing and releasing it quickly
It eliminates locks

exercises.question: What is the 'priority ceiling protocol'?
exercises.answer: Assign a ceiling priority to each lock; any task acquiring it runs at that priority
exercises.explain: The ceiling is set to the highest priority of any task that might use the lock. A task holding the lock runs at that ceiling, which limits blocking and prevents deadlock among locks.
choices: A hardware CPU feature
Assign a ceiling priority to each lock; any task acquiring it runs at that priority
A maximum priority for all tasks
A limit on how many locks exist

exercises.question: What advantage does the priority ceiling protocol have over basic priority inheritance?
exercises.answer: It bounds blocking to at most one critical section and prevents deadlock among locks
exercises.explain: With ceilings, a task can be blocked by lower-priority tasks for at most one critical section, and chains of blocking and lock deadlocks are avoided. The cost is needing to know in advance which tasks use which locks.
choices: It uses less memory
It bounds blocking to at most one critical section and prevents deadlock among locks
It is simpler to implement
It runs faster

exercises.question: Which solution is more commonly used in practice, priority inheritance or priority ceiling?
exercises.answer: Priority inheritance, because it is simpler and requires less static knowledge about locks
exercises.explain: Priority inheritance is implemented in many RTOSes (Linux real-time, VxWorks, QNX). It needs no advance analysis of which task might use which lock.
choices: Neither; other mechanisms are preferred
Both equally
Priority inheritance, because it is simpler and requires less static knowledge about locks
Priority ceiling, because it is more robust

units.title: RTOS vs General Purpose OS
units.tip: Real-Time Operating Systems are designed for predictability. General-purpose systems (Windows, Linux) prioritize throughput and flexibility. Understanding the differences explains why critical systems use dedicated RTOSes.

exercises.question: What is an RTOS?
exercises.answer: An operating system designed to handle tasks with strict timing constraints
exercises.explain: An RTOS (Real-Time Operating System) guarantees predictable latency and deadline-meeting. Examples: VxWorks, QNX, RTLinux. It trades flexibility for predictability.
choices: A Linux distribution
An operating system designed to handle tasks with strict timing constraints
An embedded system OS
Any operating system that runs fast

exercises.question: Why do many RTOSes avoid demand paging and swapping to disk?
exercises.answer: Page faults introduce unpredictable delays that violate timing guarantees
exercises.explain: Page faults and disk paging have unbounded latency. An RTOS either avoids them or tightly bounds them to maintain predictability.
choices: To save memory
RTOSes cannot use memory protection
They are too complex
Page faults introduce unpredictable delays that violate timing guarantees

exercises.question: What is 'deterministic' behavior in an RTOS?
exercises.answer: The worst-case timing of operations is known and bounded in advance
exercises.explain: Deterministic means predictable. A deterministic scheduler always completes a task in a known worst-case time, making timing guarantees possible.
choices: The behavior is always the same
The worst-case timing of operations is known and bounded in advance
The system is never random
The OS uses no algorithms

exercises.question: What is 'jitter' in an RTOS?
exercises.answer: The variation in timing between repeated executions of the same task
exercises.explain: A task that completes in 10ms one time and 11ms the next has jitter of 1ms. RTOSes minimize jitter to improve predictability.
choices: The variation in timing between repeated executions of the same task
A communication protocol
Random noise in the system
A bug in the scheduler

exercises.question: Why do RTOSes use smaller kernels than general-purpose operating systems?
exercises.answer: Smaller kernels have fewer code paths, making timing analysis and worst-case estimation easier
exercises.explain: A large, complex kernel (like Linux) has so many code paths that worst-case timing is nearly impossible to analyze. RTOSes keep the kernel minimal.
choices: To run on slower computers
Smaller kernels are always faster
To use less memory
Smaller kernels have fewer code paths, making timing analysis and worst-case estimation easier

exercises.question: What is the primary design goal of a general-purpose OS like Linux?
exercises.answer: Maximize overall throughput and allow fair resource sharing among tasks
exercises.explain: General-purpose OSes optimize for average-case performance and fairness. They may sacrifice individual task latency for overall system efficiency.
choices: Eliminate all background processes
Minimize latency for every task
Meet hard real-time deadlines
Maximize overall throughput and allow fair resource sharing among tasks

exercises.question: Why is a general-purpose OS unsuitable for hard real-time?
exercises.answer: Memory paging, cache effects, and background processes create unpredictable latencies
exercises.explain: Linux and Windows make no guarantees on task latency. A page fault, garbage collection, or background daemon can delay any task unpredictably.
choices: They use too much memory
Memory paging, cache effects, and background processes create unpredictable latencies
They cannot run user programs
They are too slow

exercises.question: What is 'preemptible Linux' or 'real-time Linux'?
exercises.answer: Linux patched to make the kernel preemptible, reducing worst-case latency to near real-time levels
exercises.explain: Projects such as PREEMPT_RT modify Linux so the kernel itself becomes preemptible, improving latency. Even so, it does not offer every guarantee of a true RTOS.
choices: A version of Linux that requires no waiting
A special Linux kernel module
Linux patched to make the kernel preemptible, reducing worst-case latency to near real-time levels
A faster version of Linux

exercises.question: What is an advantage of using Linux for soft real-time instead of a dedicated RTOS?
exercises.answer: Linux offers rich software ecosystems, drivers, and development tools
exercises.explain: Linux has vast software support. For soft real-time where occasional missed deadlines are acceptable, Linux's tools and libraries often outweigh its timing uncertainty.
choices: Linux guarantees hard real-time
Linux is faster than RTOSes
Linux uses less power
Linux offers rich software ecosystems, drivers, and development tools

exercises.question: What is an example of a commercial RTOS?
exercises.answer: VxWorks, QNX, or INTEGRITY
exercises.explain: VxWorks (Wind River) is used in aerospace and defense. QNX is popular in automotive and industrial control. INTEGRITY is used in avionics.
choices: VxWorks, QNX, or INTEGRITY
BeOS, Amiga, classic Mac OS
Windows, macOS, Linux
Android, iOS, watchOS

units.title: Temporal Properties and Latency
units.tip: Real-time systems are characterized by precise temporal properties: deadlines, latency bounds, jitter, and response times. Analyzing and measuring these properties is essential for verifying system correctness.

exercises.question: What is a 'deadline' in real-time systems?
exercises.answer: The latest time by which a task must complete and produce its result
exercises.explain: A deadline is an absolute requirement. A task triggered at time 0 with a deadline of 10ms must finish by time 10ms or the system fails.
choices: The total CPU time in the system
The latest time by which a task must complete and produce its result
How long a task has been waiting
The time it takes a task to run

exercises.question: What is 'response time' of a task?
exercises.answer: The time from when the task is triggered until it finishes execution
exercises.explain: Response time includes wait time in the queue plus actual execution time. A deadline is met if the response time does not exceed the deadline.
choices: The time between two task activations
The time from when the task is triggered until it finishes execution
How long the CPU spends on the task
The memory used by the task

exercises.question: What is 'latency' in real-time systems?
exercises.answer: The delay between an event and the system's response to that event
exercises.explain: Latency is the time from stimulus (interrupt, input) to system reaction (output, task completion). Low and predictable latency is critical.
choices: The delay between an event and the system's response to that event
The total execution time of all tasks
The time a task spends in memory
The frequency of task activations

exercises.question: What is 'interrupt latency'?
exercises.answer: The time from when an interrupt occurs until the handler begins executing
exercises.explain: Interrupt latency measures how quickly the system responds to hardware events. Long interrupt latency can cause missed deadlines.
choices: The time from when an interrupt occurs until the handler begins executing
The number of interrupts per second
The priority of an interrupt
The time an interrupt handler spends executing

exercises.question: What does 'hard deadline' mean versus 'soft deadline'?
exercises.answer: Hard: missing it causes system failure; Soft: missing it degrades service but system continues
exercises.explain: A pacemaker's hard deadline cannot be missed; a video frame's soft deadline can be occasionally missed without crashing.
choices: No practical difference
Hard: enforced by hardware, Soft: by software
Hard: missing it causes system failure; Soft: missing it degrades service but system continues
Hard: shorter, Soft: longer

exercises.question: What is 'worst-case execution time' (WCET)?
exercises.answer: The maximum time a task could possibly take under any input or system condition
exercises.explain: WCET is not the average or typical time; it is the absolute longest time. Real-time scheduling uses WCET to guarantee deadlines.
choices: The average time a task takes
The fastest a task has ever run
The maximum time a task could possibly take under any input or system condition
The time a task waits for I/O

exercises.question: How is WCET determined?
exercises.answer: By analyzing code paths, cache behavior, and running timing tests on the target hardware
exercises.explain: WCET analysis is complex. It requires understanding the worst-case path through the code, cache misses, and hardware effects. Tools and measurement combine.
choices: From the number of instructions
By analyzing code paths, cache behavior, and running timing tests on the target hardware
By running the task once
From the task name

exercises.question: What is 'jitter' in task execution?
exercises.answer: The variation between the actual response time and the expected response time
exercises.explain: If a task always takes 10ms plus or minus 1ms, it has 1ms jitter. Reducing jitter improves system predictability.
choices: The variation between the actual response time and the expected response time
The total execution time of all tasks
A bug in the scheduler
A delay in the network

exercises.question: What causes jitter in task response times?
exercises.answer: Cache hits and misses, other tasks being scheduled, and interrupt service time
exercises.explain: Jitter comes from the nondeterminism of caches, context switches, and interrupt handling. RTOSes reduce jitter by controlling these factors.
choices: Cache hits and misses, other tasks being scheduled, and interrupt service time
The task's algorithm
The operating system version
User input

exercises.question: What is 'deadline miss' defined as?
exercises.answer: A task completes after its deadline has passed
exercises.explain: If a task has a deadline of 10ms and completes at 11ms, it has missed its deadline. In hard real-time, even one miss is a failure.
choices: A task that was never scheduled
A task waiting for input
A task completes after its deadline has passed
A task that was not created

units.title: Hardware Support and Verification
units.tip: Real-time systems rely on hardware features like watchdog timers and interrupt controllers to enforce timing constraints. Verifying that a system meets its requirements requires formal methods and testing.

exercises.question: What is a 'watchdog timer'?
exercises.answer: A hardware timer that resets the system if the software does not reset it periodically
exercises.explain: A watchdog detects deadlock or infinite loops. If the system is hung and does not reset the watchdog, it times out and forces a reboot.
choices: A hardware timer that resets the system if the software does not reset it periodically
A clock that tells the time of day
A timer that measures how long a task runs
A memory protection device

exercises.question: Why would a real-time system use a watchdog timer?
exercises.answer: To automatically recover from software failures like deadlock or infinite loops
exercises.explain: In critical systems, automatic recovery is often better than waiting for human intervention. A watchdog forces a reset so the system can return to a known state.
choices: To measure power consumption
To measure execution time
To count interrupts
To automatically recover from software failures like deadlock or infinite loops

exercises.question: What is 'interrupt masking'?
exercises.answer: Disabling interrupts to execute a critical section of code without preemption
exercises.explain: By masking interrupts, a task can guarantee it is not interrupted. This is used to protect critical sections, but excessive masking violates real-time guarantees.
choices: Deleting interrupt handlers
Changing interrupt priority
Disabling interrupts to execute a critical section of code without preemption
Counting the number of interrupts

exercises.question: What problem arises if interrupts are masked for too long?
exercises.answer: Other time-critical events are delayed, potentially missing their deadlines
exercises.explain: Disabling interrupts prevents the system from responding to external events quickly. Long interrupt masks defeat real-time timing guarantees.
choices: Other time-critical events are delayed, potentially missing their deadlines
Memory is corrupted
The watchdog timer is disabled
The system runs faster

exercises.question: What is a 'timer interrupt' and why is it critical in real-time systems?
exercises.answer: A periodic interrupt from the system timer that triggers task switching and scheduling decisions
exercises.explain: Timer interrupts drive the scheduler. They occur at regular intervals (e.g., every 1ms) and allow the kernel to switch between tasks and check deadlines.
choices: A user-generated interrupt
An interrupt that stops the timer
A periodic interrupt from the system timer that triggers task switching and scheduling decisions
An interrupt from the real-time clock

exercises.question: What is 'schedulability analysis'?
exercises.answer: Mathematical analysis to prove that all tasks will meet their deadlines under a given scheduling algorithm
exercises.explain: Schedulability tests (like Liu and Layland bounds for Rate Monotonic) prove offline that the system will not miss deadlines.
choices: Measuring how fast the scheduler runs
Testing the scheduler by running the system
Checking if the scheduler has bugs
Mathematical analysis to prove that all tasks will meet their deadlines under a given scheduling algorithm

exercises.question: What is the 'Liu and Layland bound' for Rate Monotonic scheduling?
exercises.answer: A formula proving that tasks meet deadlines if their CPU utilization is below a certain threshold
exercises.explain: For n periodic tasks, if total utilization is below n(2^(1/n)-1), Rate Monotonic scheduling guarantees all deadlines are met.
choices: A way to measure jitter
A hardware requirement
A formula proving that tasks meet deadlines if their CPU utilization is below a certain threshold
A method for sorting task priorities

exercises.question: What is 'measurement-based timing analysis'?
exercises.answer: Running the system on target hardware under stress and recording the observed timings
exercises.explain: Measurement stresses the system with demanding workloads and records actual execution times. It is validation, not proof, since it only shows the cases that were observed.
choices: Drawing a timing diagram of the design
Running the system on target hardware under stress and recording the observed timings
Proving timing bounds from the code structure without running it
Predicting timing with a mathematical formula

exercises.question: Why is formal verification important for hard real-time systems?
exercises.answer: It mathematically proves the system meets requirements, not just demonstrates it in testing
exercises.explain: Testing can show that a system worked in the scenarios tried. Formal verification proves a model of the system meets its requirements in all scenarios, which is valuable when a miss is catastrophic.
choices: It mathematically proves the system meets requirements, not just demonstrates it in testing
It is faster than testing
It uses less memory
It eliminates the need for source code

exercises.question: What is a 'timing annotation' in real-time software development?
exercises.answer: Marking code with execution time estimates to support timing analysis
exercises.explain: Developers and tools annotate functions with WCET, often using pragmas or attributes, so analysis tools can build worst-case models.
choices: A note about when code was written
Marking code with execution time estimates to support timing analysis
A comment explaining the algorithm
A performance measurement
